nodes.name: Turtle grass
nodes.desc: A seagrass of shallow sandy flats. Green turtles graze it, and the meadows shelter small fish and invertebrates.

nodes.name: Halimeda algae
nodes.desc: A calcified green alga common on tropical reefs and sand. Grazers such as parrotfish, urchins and turtles feed on algae like it.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Drifting algae in the clear open water around the islands. They feed zooplankton and, through them, the fish that seabirds hunt.

nodes.name: Zooplankton
nodes.desc: Tiny drifting animals that graze phytoplankton and are eaten by small fish.

nodes.name: Flyingfish
nodes.desc: Open-water fish that feed on plankton and glide above the surface to escape predators. A classic prey of frigatebirds.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: Adults graze seagrass and algae in shallow water. Tiger sharks are their main predator.

nodes.name: Queen conch
nodes.desc: A large snail that grazes algae and plant detritus on sand and seagrass beds.

nodes.name: Stoplight parrotfish
nodes.desc: A reef fish that scrapes algae from rock and coral rubble, helping keep algae from smothering the reef.

nodes.name: Long-spined urchin
nodes.desc: A spiny urchin that grazes algae on reef surfaces.

nodes.name: Sooty tern
nodes.desc: Nests on Bush Key, the only US colony. Picks small fish from the sea surface, often far out over open water.

nodes.name: Brown pelican
nodes.desc: A plunge-diving bird that eats schooling fish around the islands and roosts on the keys.

nodes.name: Magnificent frigatebird
nodes.desc: Takes fish, often flying fish, from the surface, and also harasses other seabirds until they drop their catch.

nodes.name: Peregrine falcon
nodes.desc: A migrant visitor that hunts birds over the keys. GloBI records it eating sooty terns and ruddy turnstones.

nodes.name: Great barracuda
nodes.desc: A fast reef predator that eats fish such as flyingfish and parrotfish.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: A top predator of warm seas that eats sea turtles, fish and seabirds.

nodes.name: Bottlenose dolphin
nodes.desc: Recorded in the park waters. Hunts fish such as schooling and reef fish.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Clear, shallow water lets light reach seagrass, algae and coral on the bottom.

nodes.name: Warm clear water
nodes.desc: Warm, nutrient-poor water from the Gulf Stream system keeps the water clear. A 1977 cold snap killed about 96% of shallow branching coral here.

nodes.name: Sandy cays
nodes.desc: The park has about 144 acres of land, mostly low sand keys. Bush Key is closed in Feb to Sep to protect nesting terns and noddies.

nodes.name: Bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, algae and carcasses and return nutrients to the water and sand.
